title: WHY GOD WON’T COMPETE FOR YOUR ATTENTION
paragraphs: WHY GOD WON’T COMPETE FOR YOUR ATTENTION
The frightening thing may not be that you stopped believing in God. It may be that you still believe in Him while giving everything else the attention that belongs to Him.
There is a kind of distance from God that does not look like rebellion.
It looks like a normal day.
You wake up.
Before your feet touch the floor, your hand reaches for your phone.
Notifications.
Messages.
News.
A quick scroll that becomes twenty minutes.
Someone else's vacation. Someone else's marriage. Someone else's success. Someone else's body. Someone else's opinion. Someone else's crisis.
Your mind has barely awakened, and already a hundred voices have entered the room.
But the One who gave you another morning has not heard your voice.
You tell yourself you will pray later.
Later comes.
Work needs you.
Children need you.
Bills need paying.
Messages need answering.
Deadlines are waiting.
Something is always vibrating, ringing, refreshing, playing, demanding, reminding, advertising, entertaining.
Then night arrives.
You are exhausted.
You climb into bed and perhaps whisper a tired prayer because somewhere inside you, you still love Jesus.
And that is what makes this uncomfortable.
Because this article is not primarily about atheists.
It is about people who love God...
but have slowly trained their attention to live somewhere else.
People who would never bow before a carved idol, yet surrender hours to things they cannot stop checking.
People who would never say, "Jesus doesn't matter to me," yet repeatedly give Him whatever fragments remain after everything else has eaten.
And perhaps the most unsettling question is not:
Do you believe in Jesus?
Perhaps it is:
What receives the first, deepest, and most dependable attention of your heart?
Because whatever continually captures your attention eventually begins discipling your desires.
And whatever disciples your desires will begin shaping your life.
This is why the title of this article needs one important clarification.
When we say God won't compete for your attention, we do not mean God is incapable of defeating His competitors.
God has no equal.
He is not anxiously standing beside your phone hoping you choose Him.
He is not threatened by entertainment, success, relationships, money, ambition, algorithms, celebrities, careers, or possessions.
Scripture does not present Yahweh as one needy deity among competing gods.
It presents Him as Lord.
The issue is not God's insecurity.
The issue is God's rightful exclusivity.
After Israel's catastrophic betrayal with the golden calf, God renewed His covenant with His people. And in Exodus 34:14 we encounter startling Hebrew language:
כִּי לֹא תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה לְאֵל אַחֵר ... יְהוָה קַנָּא שְׁמוֹ אֵל קַנָּא הוּא
The central word is קַנָּא — qannāʾ, commonly translated "jealous."
God declares that His people must not worship another god because Yahweh is qannāʾ.
Jealous.
But do not import the ugliest form of human jealousy into that word.
Human jealousy can say, "I want what belongs to you."
God's covenant jealousy says, in effect, "I will not treat your idolatry as harmless because you were made to belong to Me."
The Hebrew term in these passages is used of God's demand for exclusive covenant loyalty.
This is holy jealousy.
Covenant jealousy.
The fierce love of the God who refuses to call spiritual adultery harmless.
And notice when Exodus 34 happens.
After the golden calf.
Israel had witnessed wonders.
They had watched Egypt tremble under God's judgments.
They had walked through the sea.
They had eaten God's provision.
They had seen His power.
And still...
they made something they could see, then gave it the devotion that belonged to the God who had saved them.
That should frighten every religious person reading this.
Because apparently it is possible to experience God's goodness and still manufacture substitutes for God.
Our calves are simply better designed now.
Some fit inside our pockets.
Some are called careers.
Some are called relationships.
Some are called followers.
Some are called success.
Some are called comfort.
Some are even called ministry.
An idol does not have to be something evil.
It can be something good that has quietly received what belongs ultimately to God.
Your child can become an idol.
Your spouse can become an idol.
Your dream can become an idol.
Your ministry can become an idol.
Your reputation can become an idol.
Your political obsession can become an idol.
Your need to be admired can become an idol.
Your pain can even become the center around which your entire identity begins revolving.
And yes...
your phone can become an altar without ever looking like one.
Not because smartphones are inherently sinful.
They aren't.
Neither are careers, hobbies, entertainment, possessions, or social media inherently sinful.
The deeper question is whether something has begun commanding your heart.
What can you not imagine losing?
What determines whether you feel valuable?
Where does your mind instinctively run when silence arrives?
What gets your first attention?
What receives your best energy?
What makes you feel alive?
What are you willing to disobey God to keep?
There.
That last question hurts.
Because idolatry is eventually exposed not merely by what we enjoy...
but by what we refuse to surrender.
Jesus once entered a home where two sisters responded very differently to His presence.
Martha was serving.
That matters.
She was not committing some obvious scandal.
She was doing something useful.
Something hospitable.
Something respectable.
Yet Luke tells us she was distracted by her serving.
Jesus answered her tenderly:
"Martha, Martha..."
Then He exposed the condition underneath the activity.
She was anxious and troubled about many things, while Mary had chosen the good portion.
Don't miss this.
Martha's problem was not that she was serving Jesus.
Her problem was that serving Jesus had somehow distracted her from Jesus.
Read that again.
Because some Christians are doing exactly this.
You can sing about Jesus while your heart is elsewhere.
You can post Scripture while your private life starves.
You can defend Christianity online while barely speaking to Christ.
You can serve at church while secretly becoming spiritually hollow.
You can build a ministry around Jesus while gradually losing intimacy with Jesus.
You can spend your life discussing Him...
and stop sitting at His feet.
That is one of the most terrifying possibilities in Christianity.
Being busy around Jesus while becoming distant from Jesus.
And the world is extraordinarily good at keeping you busy.
Not necessarily wicked.
Just busy.
Distracted.
Fragmented.
Overstimulated.
Always consuming.
Always reacting.
Always moving.
Never still long enough to notice what is happening inside your soul.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe you haven't abandoned God.
You are simply distracted.
And distraction feels innocent because there was never a dramatic moment when you decided to walk away.
There was no declaration.
No slammed Bible.
No conscious renunciation of Christ.
Just...
tomorrow.
"I'll pray tomorrow."
"I'll read Scripture tomorrow."
"I'll deal with that sin tomorrow."
"I'll forgive them tomorrow."
"I'll repent tomorrow."
"I'll return to church tomorrow."
"I'll get serious about Jesus tomorrow."
And tomorrow became months.
Maybe years.
Until one day you realized you could remember when your heart used to burn for God.
You remember worship that once broke you.
You remember opening Scripture hungry.
You remember conviction arriving quickly.
You remember wanting holiness more than applause.
You remember when prayer was not merely something you did when your life fell apart.
But now...
you scroll.
You consume.
You laugh.
You work.
You perform.
You survive.
And somewhere underneath all the noise is a frightening ache:
What happened to me?
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not answer that question by telling you to become impressive enough for God to take you back.
Christianity is not the story of distracted sinners finally becoming disciplined enough to climb their way to God.
It is the story of God coming for sinners.
Jesus Christ entered our world.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He resisted temptation.
He loved the Father perfectly.
He obeyed where we rebelled.
Then He went to a cross.
And there the scandal becomes grace.
Because the cross reveals something devastating about sin:
Sin is worse than we wanted to admit.
And the cross simultaneously reveals something breathtaking about God's mercy:
His grace is greater than we dared hope.
Jesus endured the cross and its shame. Hebrews 12:2 places before us this extraordinary Greek expression:
ἀφορῶντες εἰς ... Ἰησοῦν
aphorōntes eis ... Iēsoun
Looking to Jesus.

The verb carries the sense of directing one's gaze toward Him. Hebrews calls Christ the pioneer and perfecter of faith and points to His endurance of the cross before His exaltation at God's right hand.
Do you see the beauty?
The answer to a distracted soul is ultimately not merely:
Look at your screen less.
It is:
Look to Jesus.
Because Christianity cannot be reduced to digital minimalism.
You could throw your phone into the ocean and still worship yourself.
You could delete every social-media account and still idolize money.
You could live alone in the mountains and still be consumed by pride.
The deepest problem is not the device in your hand.
It is the throne in your heart.
And only one King belongs there.
Jesus.
This is where repentance becomes beautiful.
Repentance is not God screaming, "Do better!"
Repentance is the gracious summons to turn.
Come home.
Bring Him the divided heart.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the secret compromise.
Bring Him the prayerlessness.
Bring Him the nights you wasted.
Bring Him the hidden browser history.
Bring Him the ambition you worshiped.
Bring Him the relationship you made ultimate.
Bring Him the image you have spent years protecting.
Bring Him the part of yourself you are terrified anyone will discover.
Bring Him your scandal.
Because Jesus has always been in the business of rewriting stories people thought were finished.
Peter denied Him.
Christ restored Peter.
Thomas doubted.
Christ met Thomas.
A thief was dying beside Him with nothing left to offer.
Christ gave him hope.
Paul had persecuted the church.
Christ turned the persecutor into a preacher of the Gospel.
Again and again Scripture tells the same impossible story:
Sin does not get the final sentence when Jesus enters the story.
Failure does not get the final sentence.
Shame does not get the final sentence.
Your past does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Grace is not permission to continue worshiping your idols.
Grace breaks their claim over you and calls you back to the living God.
So perhaps the question tonight is not whether God can get your attention.
Perhaps He already has.
Perhaps that strange discomfort you feel while reading this is the moment when the noise has finally become quiet enough for you to recognize what your soul has been missing.
Jesus.
Not merely Christian content.
Jesus.
Not religious motivation.
Jesus.
Not another inspirational quotation.
Jesus.
Not an emotional experience that disappears tomorrow morning.
Jesus Christ crucified, risen, reigning, forgiving sinners, receiving the repentant, transforming lives.
Maybe you need to put the phone down after this.
Maybe you need to open your Bible.
Maybe you need to kneel beside your bed.
Maybe you need to confess something you have spent months defending.
Maybe there is an app you need to delete because you know exactly what it keeps doing to you.
Maybe there is a relationship you have elevated above obedience to Christ.
Maybe success has become your functional savior.
Maybe people's approval has become your oxygen.
Maybe you have been feeding everyone else's perception of you while starving your soul.
Whatever it is, do not turn this into vague guilt.
Take it to Christ.
Name it.
Confess it.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
And look again to Jesus.
You do not need to earn His cross.
You cannot.
You need the mercy purchased there.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, don't pretend it didn't.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need prayer is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building around ourselves.
Not to embarrass them.
Send this to the friend whose faith has become tired.
There is also something important I want to say about supporting this work.
Supporting Gospel ministry is a worthy act when it flows from love for Christ, generosity, and a desire to help biblical truth reach people.
It doesn't.
You do not glorify God by being pressured into paying for something.
You glorify God by belonging to Christ and faithfully obeying Him.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, encouraging, and putting Gospel-centered material in front of people who may desperately need it.
The goal is not to create consumers.
It is to help cultivate disciples.
People who know Scripture.
People who pray.
People who repent.
People who forgive.
People who endure.
People who refuse to make peace with hidden sin.
People whose eyes keep returning to Christ.
And comment.
Be honest.
What has been competing for your attention lately?
You don't have to tell your entire story.
Maybe your answer is "work."
"Money."
"My phone."
"A relationship."
"Pornography."
"Approval."
"Success."
"Fear."
"Myself."
Or simply:
"Jesus, take back my attention."
There may be another believer reading the comments who thought they were the only one fighting the same battle.
Your honesty may become somebody else's courage.
Because somewhere tonight, another person is staring into the glow of a screen while carrying a soul that is starving for eternity.
Maybe they will see what you shared.
Maybe they will remember Jesus.
Maybe they will come home.
And perhaps that is worth one share.
Because eventually every notification will disappear.
Every trend will die.
Every possession will belong to somebody else.
Every applause will become silent.
Every follower count will become meaningless.
Every screen will go dark.
And the question will never have been whether God was worthy of your attention.
He always was.
The question is what you did with the brief life in which He gave you the opportunity to know Him.
So come back.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Look away from the thousand things begging to become your master...
and look again to Jesus.
Because the tragedy is not merely that the world stole your attention—it is that Christ was worthy of your whole heart while you were giving Him the leftovers.
